The story behind an idea

Phrenology: reading the mind in the bumps of the skull

It was a 19th-century fad and a pseudoscience, but it left behind a correct idea: different brain areas do different things.

The German physician Franz Joseph Gall (1758–1828) proposed that the brain was made up of "organs" responsible for faculties such as friendship, destructiveness or love of offspring. The more developed one was, the more the skull would bulge in that area. His collaborator Spurzheim popularised the term phrenology.

Fashion and fall

It became hugely popular in Europe and America: phrenologists examined heads to give career advice or help choose a partner. In Spain it was spread by Mariano Cubí i Soler in the 1840s. But Pierre Flourens's experiments on animals found no such organs, and scientists abandoned it.

A 2018 study using brain scans of thousands of people confirmed, in case any doubt remained, that skull shape is unrelated to abilities. Even so, phrenology left an idea that Broca and others later confirmed with scientific methods: mental functions are partly localised in different brain regions.

References

  1. Parker Jones, O., Alfaro-Almagro, F. y Jbabdi, S. (2018). An empirical, 21st century evaluation of phrenology. Cortex, 106, 26–35.
  2. van Wyhe, J. (2004). Phrenology and the Origins of Victorian Scientific Naturalism. Ashgate.
